title: Packages and Access Modifiers
description: Organizing classes into packages, importing them, and the four access levels revisited in that context.
objectives: Understand how access modifiers interact with package structure

content.heading: Declaring and Importing Packages
content.body: A package groups related classes together and creates a namespace, avoiding naming collisions between classes from different parts of a large project or different libraries entirely. A file declares its package with package com.example.banking; as its very first line (before any import or class declaration), and the containing directory structure must physically match the package name (com/example/banking/). To use a class from a different package, either import its fully-qualified name (import java.util.ArrayList;) or reference it fully qualified inline (java.util.ArrayList list = ...), without an import at all. import java.util.*; imports every class in that package (a wildcard import), generally discouraged in favor of explicit imports for clarity, though harmless functionally.

content.heading: Access Modifiers in Package Context
content.body: Revisiting the four access levels through the lens of packages: private is visible only within the declaring class. Package-private (no modifier) is visible to any class within the same package, but not from outside it — useful for helper classes/methods meant only for internal use within a module. protected is visible within the same package and also to subclasses in other packages (an important nuance: it's package-private plus subclass access, not simply 'more open than package-private in every direction'). public is visible everywhere. Well-organized packages, combined with careful choice of access levels, form the backbone of a maintainable large Java codebase — deciding what's part of a package's public API versus its internal implementation detail.

content.explanation: This example spans two separate source files (marked by the // File: comments) to show how package/directory structure and import work together — it is not meant to compile as a single file. Account.java's directory (com/example/banking/) matches its package declaration exactly, and Main.java, in a different package, needs the import statement to reference Account by its simple name.

keyPoints: package declares a class's namespace; the directory structure must match the package name
import brings a class from another package into scope by its simple name
Package-private (no modifier) restricts access to classes in the same package only
protected extends package-private access to subclasses in other packages as well
commonMistakes: Mismatching the package declaration and the actual directory structure
Overusing wildcard imports (import java.util.*;), reducing clarity about exactly what's used
Assuming protected is simply 'wider than package-private' in every direction, rather than package-private-plus-subclasses specifically
